358.title: The blind men and the elephant
358.word: The blind men and the elephant
358.hook: each man touches one part of the elephant and quarrels with the rest (Udana 6.4)
358.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers tell the story of the blind men and the elephant to warn against clinging to partial views and quarreling over them, and it is widely told in other traditions too.

segments.voice: Yesterday: views held lightly, and your line, a raft, not a house. Did you catch yourself carrying a view on your head in a disagreement? Day three hundred fifty-eight.
screen: `VIEWS HELD LIGHTLY — A RAFT, NOT A HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Year two began with an elephant's footprint. Right view ends with the whole elephant. In the city of Savatthi, the monks come back from their alms round shaken. All over town, teachers and their followers are arguing about the big questions: is the world eternal, is the soul the body. Each side says, only this is true, everything else is foolish. The arguing has turned into shouting, and the shouting into wounding words. The monks tell the Buddha. He doesn't answer by declaring a winner. He tells them about a king who once borrowed an elephant.
screen: `MONKS COME BACK SHAKEN.` → `ONLY THIS IS TRUE.` → `A KING BORROWS AN ELEPHANT.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Udana, a short book of inspired sayings, chapter six. Long ago, the Buddha says, a king of Savatthi had his servant gather every man in the city who had been born blind. Then he had an elephant brought, and let each man touch one part. To some he showed the head, to some the ear, the tusk, the trunk, the body, the foot, the back, the tail, the tuft at the end of the tail. Then the king asked: what is an elephant like? The ones who touched the head said: like a water pot. The ear: a winnowing basket. The tusk: a plowshare. The trunk: a plow pole. The body: a storehouse. The foot: a post. The back: a mortar. The tail: a pestle. The tuft: a broom. And then, the text says, they began to argue, each insisting, the elephant is like this, not like that, until they came to blows. And the king was delighted. The Buddha says the quarreling teachers are like this: they don't see the whole, and so they fight over the part. Notice whom the story is aimed at: anyone, of any group, who seizes a part and calls it the whole, including his own monks. The ten big questions in the background are the same ones Malunkyaputta wanted answered, the ones left aside in the arrow story. This story has neighbors: Jains, Hindus and Sufi poets like Rumi tell their own versions, each with its own lesson. In the Udana, the lesson closes the section on right view: each holds a part.
screen: `A KING GATHERS THE BLIND.` · `A POT, A BASKET, A BROOM.` · `THEY COME TO BLOWS.` · `SEIZING A PART AS THE WHOLE.` · then, large: `EACH HOLDS A PART.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to hear out one view you dislike. Sit, and bring to mind a view held by someone you disagree with. Not to adopt it. Just to touch it. Ask: what part of the elephant might they be holding? What did they touch that I didn't? Breathe with that question a few times. If irritation comes, notice it, and come back to the breath. Let both your part and theirs be parts. The bell holds the time.
The blind men and the elephant. Each touches one part and fights over the whole: the Buddha's picture of clinging to partial views.
screen: `THE BLIND MEN AND THE ELEPHANT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: each holds a part. Today, in one conversation where you disagree, ask the other person one honest question about what they see, and listen to the whole answer. Day three hundred fifty-eight.

match.prompt: match each part of the elephant to what it seemed like.

Jains, Hindus and Sufi poets like Rumi tell versions too, each with its own lesson.

options: he stops the fight and explains the whole elephant.
he is delighted.
he sends the elephant away.
fork.reveal: the text says the king was delighted; the Buddha uses the scene to show how people who see only one side wrangle.

original.note: Pali jaccandha: born blind; the king gathers the jaccandhā of Savatthi.

trapdoor: what you thought: the story says every view is equally right.
what it means: in the Udana, it warns against seizing one part and fighting over it as the whole.

what a scholar hears: Udana 6.4 (Tittha Sutta) is set against wanderers quarreling over the ten undeclared points; Jain, Hindu and Sufi versions (Rumi's Masnavi has an elephant in a dark room) draw their own morals.

sources.ref: Udana 6.4 (Tittha Sutta, the blind men and the elephant)

359.title: Right intention
359.hook: intentions of letting go, of goodwill, of harmlessness (MN 117)
359.howItsDone: Many Buddhists set an intention at the start of the day, a meditation or a retreat, and teachers often present right intention through its three parts: renunciation, goodwill and harmlessness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the blind men and the elephant, and your line, each holds a part. Did you ask someone one honest question about what they see? Day three hundred fifty-nine.
screen: `THE BLIND MEN AND THE ELEPHANT — EACH HOLDS A PART.`

segments.voice: Two people hand you a cup of coffee. Same cup, same coffee, same smile. One is doing it because they care whether your morning goes well. The other is doing it because they want something from you this afternoon. From the outside, there's no difference at all. From the inside, they're walking two different roads. That inside part, the aim behind the act, is the second spoke of the wheel. After right view comes the question: now that you see, what are you aiming at? Today, right intention.
screen: `TWO CUPS OF COFFEE.` → `SAME CUP, DIFFERENT AIM.` → `WHAT ARE YOU AIMING AT?`

segments.voice: The Pali is samma sankappa. Sankappa means thought, intention, resolve: what the mind is set on. Rhys Davids, translating the first sermon in 1881, called it right aspiration. The suttas define it in three parts, in the Great Forty and in the sutta that lists all eight factors. Right intention is the intention of letting go, the intention of goodwill, and the intention of harmlessness. Letting go, nekkhamma, is the aim of wanting less, of not being run by craving. Goodwill is the aim of wishing others well instead of ill. Harmlessness is the aim of not causing pain, the root of compassion. Three aims, and each one is the medicine for a particular poison: letting go for greed, goodwill for ill will, harmlessness for cruelty. Notice where right intention sits. With right view, it makes up the training in wisdom. That can seem odd: isn't intention about will, not wisdom? But in the Buddha's teaching, seeing clearly and aiming well belong together. Once you see that craving causes dukkha, you start to aim away from it. And intention matters because it shapes everything after it. The Dhammapada opens, in Max Müller's 1881 translation: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." The Pali word there is different, but the point is close: the mind goes first. Right intention isn't a promise to be perfect. It's choosing the direction the cup of coffee comes from.
screen: `SANKAPPA: WHAT THE MIND IS SET ON.` · `LETTING GO, GOODWILL, HARMLESSNESS.` · `PART OF THE TRAINING IN WISDOM.` · `THE MIND GOES FIRST.` · then, large: `INTEND IT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to set one intention now. Sit and let the breath settle. Choose one of the three: letting go, goodwill, or harmlessness. Let it become a short phrase in your own words, something like: today, I'll want a little less; or, today, I'll wish people well; or, today, I won't add to anyone's pain. Breathe it in and out a few times. Don't make it a vow. Just point the compass. The bell holds the time.
Samma sankappa. Right intention: aiming at letting go, at goodwill, and at harmlessness. The second factor of the path.
Your line: intend it. Today, before one ordinary act, a text, a meeting, a meal, take a breath and choose the aim behind it. Day three hundred fifty-nine.

with right view, it makes up the training in wisdom.

fork.setup: two people hand you identical cups of coffee. one cares about your morning; one wants a favor later. by today's teaching, where's the difference?
options: in the coffee.

fork.reveal: the act looks the same; right intention is about the aim behind it, which shapes everything that follows.

original.note: Pali sammā saṅkappa: right intention or right resolve, the second factor of the eightfold path.

trapdoor: what you thought: intention doesn't matter, only results.
what it means: in the Buddha's teaching the aim behind an act is its own factor of the path.
what a scholar hears: SN 45.8 and MN 117 define sammā saṅkappa as nekkhamma-, abyāpāda- and avihiṃsā-saṅkappa; Rhys Davids rendered it right aspirations in SBE XI.

sources.ref: MN 117 (Mahacattarisaka Sutta) and SN 45.8 (Vibhanga Sutta), right intention defined

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)

360.title: Two piles
360.hook: before his awakening he sorted his thoughts into two kinds (MN 19)
360.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist schools teach students to notice thoughts as wholesome or unwholesome and to see where they lead, a method drawn from the Dvedhavitakka Sutta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma sankappa, right intention, and your line, intend it. Did you choose the aim behind one ordinary act? Day three hundred sixty.

Cleaning out a closet usually comes down to two piles. Keep, and let go. You pick up a sweater, hold it for a second, and drop it on one side or the other. It's slow at first. After an hour you're fast, because your hands have learned what belongs where. Most of the Buddha's teachings come after his awakening. This one is different. In it he looks back to the years before, when he was still searching, and tells the monks about a simple experiment he ran on his own mind. Two piles. Today, the sutta of two kinds of thought.
screen: `CLEANING OUT A CLOSET.` → `KEEP, AND LET GO.` → `AN EXPERIMENT ON HIS OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: The sutta is number nineteen in the Middle-Length Discourses. Its name means two kinds of thought. Before my awakening, the Buddha says, while I was still a bodhisatta, it occurred to me: what if I divide my thoughts into two classes? On one side he put thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty. On the other: thoughts of letting go, thoughts of goodwill, and thoughts of harmlessness. You'll recognize the second pile. It's exactly yesterday's right intention, three aims. Then he watched. When a thought from the first pile came up, he didn't fight it or shame himself. He looked at where it led. He saw that it led to his own affliction, to others' affliction, to both; that it blocked wisdom and led away from peace. And as he saw that, the sutta says, the thought faded. When a thought from the second pile came up, he saw that it led to no one's harm, and helped wisdom grow. Then comes the line that makes this sutta famous. Whatever someone keeps thinking about and pondering, the Buddha says, that becomes the leaning of their mind. Think often about ill will, and the mind leans toward ill will. Think often about goodwill, and it leans toward goodwill. Like a path worn across a field, or a closet that sorts itself faster every time. Notice how humble the method is. No special state required. Just noticing which pile a thought belongs in, and where it's heading. A practice from before the awakening, offered to anyone.
screen: `BEFORE MY AWAKENING.` · `DESIRE, ILL WILL, CRUELTY.` · `WHERE DOES THIS THOUGHT LEAD?` · `WHAT YOU PONDER, THE MIND LEANS TO.` · then, large: `TWO PILES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sort today's thoughts in two. Sit, and simply watch thoughts come and go. As each one passes, gently drop it on a side. Does this one lean toward wanting, resentment, or harm? First pile. Does it lean toward letting go, goodwill, or kindness? Second pile. If you can't tell, let it pass unsorted. Don't argue with any thought. Just notice which way it leans. The bell holds the time.
Two piles. The Buddha's practice before awakening: sorting thoughts into those that lead to harm and those that lead to good, because the mind leans toward what it ponders.
Your line: two piles. Today, when a thought keeps returning, ask which pile it belongs in, and where it would lead if you followed it. Day three hundred sixty.

pairs: the sutta of two kinds of thought
becomes the leaning of the mind

he says he did it before, while still a bodhisatta.

options: shame yourself for having it.

fork.reveal: he saw that it led to his own and others' affliction and away from wisdom, and as he saw that, it subsided.

original.note: Pali dvedhāvitakka: two kinds of thought, the title of MN 19; vitakka means thought.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation means stopping all thoughts.
what it means: here it means sorting thoughts by where they lead, and letting the mind lean toward the good.

what a scholar hears: MN 19 sets kāma-, byāpāda- and vihiṃsā-vitakka against nekkhamma-, abyāpāda- and avihiṃsā-vitakka, and states yaññad eva bahulam anuvitakketi... tathā tathā nati hoti cetaso: the mind inclines to what is often thought.

sources.ref: MN 19 (Dvedhavitakka Sutta, two kinds of thought)

361.title: The cowherd in autumn
361.hook: a cowherd guards the ripe crops with a stick, then rests under a tree once the harvest is in (MN 19)
361.howItsDone: Meditation teachers often describe a balance of effort and ease, sometimes using the cowherd of MN 19: careful guarding of the mind at first, then relaxed awareness once the mind has settled.

segments.voice: Yesterday: two piles, and your line, two piles. Did you notice which pile a returning thought belonged in, and where it was heading? Today, the same sutta, and its cowherd. Day three hundred sixty-one.

Late in the rainy season in northern India, the rice stands tall and green right up to the edge of the village paths. It's beautiful, and for a cowherd it's a nightmare. His cows want nothing more than to wander into those fields and eat. If they do, the farmer will have him fined, or beaten, or blamed in front of everyone. So all day long he walks beside them with a stick, tapping and turning them back. Then the harvest comes in, the fields are bare, and everything changes. In the sutta of two kinds of thought, the Buddha says his mind was like those cows. Today, the cowherd in two seasons.
screen: `THE RICE STANDS TALL.` → `COWS WANT THE FIELDS.` → `A COWHERD WITH A STICK.`

segments.voice: Here's the first season, from the Middle-Length Discourses, number nineteen. In the last month of the rains, in autumn, when the crops are ripening, a cowherd guards his cows by tapping and poking them this way and that with a stick. Why? Because he sees the trouble that will come if they stray into the crops. In the same way, the Buddha says, he saw the danger in unwholesome thoughts, and the blessing in letting them go. That's the guarding: yesterday's two piles, done with attention, the stick tapping when the mind wanders toward ill will or craving. Then something surprising. He says that even wholesome thinking, if he kept it up too long, would tire his body, and a tired body strains the mind. So he steadied his mind inside, quieted it, and brought it together. And here's the second season. In the last month of the hot season, when all the crops have been brought into the village, the cowherd guards his cows while sitting at the foot of a tree or out in the open. He only needs to be aware: there are the cows. No stick. No running. That, the Buddha says, was all he needed then: simple awareness that those states were there. Two lessons sit in this one picture. First, guarding the mind takes effort at the start, and that's fine. Second, effort isn't the whole path. There comes a time to put the stick down and rest under the tree, still aware, but at ease. Teachers often say beginners grip too hard. The cowherd in autumn knows both seasons.
screen: `AUTUMN: A STICK AND THE RIPE CROPS.` · `EVEN GOOD THINKING TIRES.` · `HOT SEASON: REST UNDER A TREE.` · `EFFORT, THEN EASE.` · then, large: `GUARD, THEN REST.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to guard, then relax. For the first half of the sit, be the cowherd in autumn. Watch the breath closely, and each time the mind wanders, tap it gently back. Then, about halfway, let the stick go. Imagine sitting at the foot of a tree with the fields bare. Simply know: there's the breath, there are the thoughts. Nothing to herd. Just aware, and at ease. The bell holds the time.
The cowherd in autumn. Guarding the mind with care while the crops are ripe, then resting under a tree, simply aware, once the harvest is in.
Your line: guard, then rest. Today, give one task your full, careful effort, and when it's done, actually rest, without grabbing the next thing. Day three hundred sixty-one.

fork.reveal: with no crops to protect, he rests at the foot of a tree, mindful that the cows are there; the Buddha says his mind needed only that awareness.

original.note: Pali gopālaka: a cowherd, from go, cow, and pāla, keeper.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation is constant effort to control the mind.
what it means: guard the mind when it needs guarding, then rest in simple awareness.

what a scholar hears: MN 19 uses two cowherd similes, the autumn (sarada) month with the stick and the last month of the hot season (gimha) at the tree's root, framing the move from restraining thought to the stillness that leads into jhāna.

sources.ref: MN 19 (Dvedhavitakka Sutta), the two cowherd similes

362.title: Letting go
362.hook: renunciation as the relief of wanting less, not grim denial
362.howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice letting go in small doses: on observance days lay people may keep eight precepts, skipping the evening meal and entertainment, and in some Theravada countries many men ordain as monks for a short time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the cowherd in autumn, and your line, guard then rest. Once the guarding was done, did you let yourself rest under the tree for a minute? Day three hundred sixty-two.
screen: `THE COWHERD IN AUTUMN — GUARD, THEN REST.`

segments.voice: Moving day. You're carrying the twelfth box down the stairs, and you open it to find chargers for phones you haven't owned in ten years. You drop the whole box at the donation bin, and something odd happens. Your shoulders come down. You feel lighter, and not only in the arms. Nobody would call that grim. Nobody would call it a sacrifice. It just feels like relief. That feeling, in miniature, is the first thought in the Buddha's good pile, the one from two days ago, and it has a name that usually gets translated badly. Today: letting go.
screen: `THE TWELFTH BOX.` → `DROPPED AT THE BIN.` → `YOUR SHOULDERS COME DOWN.`

segments.voice: The word is nekkhamma, usually translated renunciation, and renunciation sounds like a monk in a cold cell refusing soup. The Pali word is tied to going out, the same family as the going forth of someone who leaves home to become a monk or nun. But in the suttas it also names a thought anyone can have: the thought of putting something down. In the sutta of the two kinds of thought, the Buddha remembers sorting his thinking, before his awakening, into two piles. In one: sensual wanting, ill will, harming. In the other: letting go, goodwill, not harming. Letting go comes first in the good pile. Here's the honest part. In another sutta, a householder named Tapussa tells Ananda that letting go looks, to people like him, like a cliff edge. The Buddha's answer is surprising. Before his awakening, he says, he too thought renunciation was good, yet his heart didn't leap at it. It only did once he had truly seen the trouble that wanting brings, and tasted the ease of not wanting. So the tradition doesn't say grit your teeth. It says look closely until the relief becomes real to you. The Dhammapada frames it as a trade, in Max Müller's words: "If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great." And nekkhamma isn't only for monks. In Theravada lists of the ten perfections it is the third, and lay people practice it in small doses, keeping eight precepts on an observance day. Less, chosen freely, can feel like more room.
screen: `NEKKHAMMA: THE THOUGHT OF PUTTING DOWN.` · `FIRST IN THE GOOD PILE.` · `TAPUSSA: IT LOOKS LIKE A CLIFF.` · `LOOK UNTIL THE RELIEF IS REAL.` · then, large: `THE RELIEF OF LESS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one thing you want right now. Not a big life want. Something small and live: the next snack, the reply to a message, a purchase waiting in a cart. Notice how the wanting sits in the body, a lean forward, a little tightness somewhere. Now, just for these two minutes, put it down. You can pick it up later if you choose. Watch what the body does when you set it down. If there's any relief, rest in it. The bell holds the time.
Nekkhamma. Letting go, renunciation: the thought of putting something down, first in the good pile, felt as relief rather than loss.
Your line: the relief of less. Today, put down one want, a purchase, a second helping, an argument you were planning to win, and notice how you feel an hour later. Day three hundred sixty-two.

fork.reveal: in AN 9.41 the Buddha says that before his awakening his heart didn't leap at renunciation either; it did once he had seen the drawbacks of sensual wanting and tasted the ease of letting go.

original.note: Pali nekkhamma (Sanskrit naiṣkramya): letting go, renunciation, from the same family as going forth.

363.title: Goodwill
363.hook: the intention of non-ill-will: metta as a steering wheel
363.howItsDone: Buddhists across traditions practice mettā, often by repeating short phrases of goodwill toward themselves, loved ones, strangers and difficult people; many monastics recite the simile of the saw as a reminder of patience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nekkhamma, letting go, and your line, the relief of less. Did you put one want down, and how did you feel an hour later? Day three hundred sixty-three.

In the city of Savatthi, the Buddha says, there lived a lady of the house named Vedehika, and everyone said the same thing about her: so gentle, so calm, so peaceful. Her maid, Kali, wondered whether that was true, or whether Vedehika had simply never been given a reason to be otherwise. So Kali tested her. One morning she got up late. Vedehika scowled. The next morning, later still. Sharp words. The third morning Kali slept in again, and her famously gentle mistress grabbed a rolling pin and hit her on the head. Kali ran out bleeding and told the whole street. Today: goodwill, and how to steer with it.
screen: `SO GENTLE, EVERYONE SAID.` → `THE MAID SLEEPS IN.` → `THE THIRD MORNING.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells that story in the sutta of the simile of the saw, and his point is sharp: a person is gentle only until disagreeable words reach them. Being calm when nobody pushes doesn't prove much. That's why the second right intention is goodwill. In Pali it's abyāpāda, literally non-ill-will, and the suttas fill it in with mettā, loving-kindness. Notice what kind of thing it is. Not a warm feeling that washes over you when it feels like it. An intention: a direction you set. Think of a steering wheel. The road throws things at you, a rude email, a driver who cuts in, a relative who says the thing. You don't control the road. You do have your hands on the wheel, and goodwill is which way you turn it. The same sutta then goes about as far as a teaching can go. Even if bandits were to cut you limb from limb with a two-handled saw, the Buddha says, anyone whose mind filled with hate would not be carrying out his teaching. He tells the monks to train so their minds stay unshaken, they speak no evil words, and they stay with goodwill toward that very person, and from there toward the whole world. Most of us will never meet those bandits. We'll meet the slow line at the pharmacy and the group chat. That may be why the same sutta opens with Vedehika and closes with the saw. The test usually comes in small, ordinary pushes, and each one is a turn of the wheel.
screen: `GENTLE UNTIL SOMEONE PUSHES.` · `ABYĀPĀDA: NON-ILL-WILL.` · `GOODWILL IS A STEERING WHEEL.` · `EVEN UNDER THE SAW.` · then, large: `STEER BY GOODWILL.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Think of a conversation you'll probably have today, one with a little friction in it. Picture the moment where it usually goes sideways. Rest your hands lightly, as if on a wheel. Now, before it begins, set the direction: whatever they say, turn toward their good. Not agreeing with everything. Just the direction. Breathe with that. If the old irritation shows up in the picture, notice it, and turn the wheel gently back. The bell holds the time.
Goodwill. Abyāpāda, non-ill-will, the second kind of right intention: not a mood but a direction you set, close kin to mettā.
Your line: steer by goodwill. Today, choose one conversation and steer it kindly, especially at the moment it pushes back. Day three hundred sixty-three.

it's an intention, a direction you set: abyāpāda, non-ill-will.

MN 21 says a mind filled with hate even then isn't carrying out the teaching.
Vedehika was known for her short temper

original.note: Pali abyāpāda: non-ill-will, the second of the three right intentions, filled in by the suttas with mettā.

364.title: Harmlessness
364.hook: the intention not to harm, even in thought
364.howItsDone: Buddhists keep the first precept, not killing, as the outward form of harmlessness; many also recite or reflect on verses like Dhammapada 129 and practice compassion meditation toward beings who suffer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: goodwill, and your line, steer by goodwill. Did one conversation get steered kindly, even a little, when it pushed back? Day three hundred sixty-four, the end of the week.

Someone cuts in front of you in traffic, or takes credit for your work, and a little film starts playing in your head. In the film, they trip on the stairs. Their coffee spills down their shirt. Their car gets a flat in the rain. Nobody is badly hurt, of course. Just enough. You'd never do any of it. You might not even notice the film is running. The Buddha noticed. Before his awakening, he says, he caught thoughts of harming in his own mind and put them in the bad pile, right beside ill will. Today, the last of the three right intentions: harmlessness, all the way down into thought.
screen: `SOMEONE CUTS IN.` → `A LITTLE FILM STARTS.` → `JUST ENOUGH HARM.`

segments.voice: The word on our list is ahimsa, the Sanskrit form most people know, the not-harming that Jains and Hindus hold dear as well. In the Pali list of right intentions, the word is avihiṃsā, non-cruelty: the intention not to harm. Yesterday's goodwill was about not wishing ill. This one leans closer to action: not wanting anyone to suffer, and not wanting to be the cause. In the sutta of the two kinds of thought, the Buddha is plain about thoughts of harming. When one arose in him, he saw that it led to his own affliction, to the affliction of others, or to both, and that it led away from wisdom. Seeing that clearly, he says, it faded. So harm starts upstream, in the film, long before a hand moves. The Dhammapada gives the reason in one line, in Max Müller's words: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter." You are like them. That's the whole argument. A later verse says a person isn't called noble for injuring living creatures, but for having pity on all of them. In the tradition's way of thinking, harmlessness is the soil compassion grows in. Look back at the week. The blind men, each holding a part. Intend it. Two piles. Guard, then rest. The relief of less. Steer by goodwill. And today, no harm meant. Three right intentions, one direction.
screen: `AVIHIṂSĀ: THE INTENTION NOT TO HARM.` · `HARM STARTS UPSTREAM.` · `YOU ARE LIKE THEM.` · `THE SOIL COMPASSION GROWS IN.` · then, large: `NO HARM MEANT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath find its own pace. Now, gently, look for the film. Is there anyone you've been quietly wishing a small misfortune on? A coworker, a neighbor, someone on the news? Don't scold yourself for finding it. Just catch it, the way you'd catch a glass before it hits the floor. Then do what the Dhammapada suggests: remember they're like you. They flinch at pain too. Let the film stop there. The bell holds the time.
Ahimsa. Not harming. In the Buddha's list it's avihiṃsā, the intention not to harm, the third right intention.
Your line: no harm meant. Today, catch one harmful thought before the film finishes, and let it end unfinished. Day three hundred sixty-four, and a week done.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali ahiṃsā: not harming; the Pali right-intention list uses its close cousin avihiṃsā, non-cruelty.
